title: AI Helps Scientists Understand How Cells Talk
summary:
Every body starts as a tiny group of stem cells. Slowly, these cells turn into different kinds, like brain, liver or muscle cells.

Cells do not decide alone. They send chemical messages to their neighbors. These messages move along paths called signaling pathways. The messages change which genes in the cell are switched on.

Scientists at MIT, led by Pulin Li and Nicholas Hutchins, found that each pathway leaves a special "fingerprint" in the cell. The same pathway leaves the same kind of fingerprint in many types of cells.

The team built an AI model called IRIS to find these fingerprints. Li compared it to Siri, which learns English and then uses that to understand other languages.

IRIS correctly guessed the signals in mouse cells that would become heart, gut, muscle and spinal cord. It also helped find a signal for making lung cells. This could help scientists grow better lab models of organs to study diseases.
why_it_matters: Learning how cells talk could one day help doctors understand and treat diseases.

keywords.explanation: Stem cells are starter cells that can grow into many different kinds of cells.
A chemical is a substance, and cells use some chemicals like messages.
Signaling pathways are paths that carry messages into a cell and tell it what to do.
Genes are tiny instructions inside cells that help decide how a body grows.
An AI model is a computer program that learns patterns from lots of information.
